mcq.q: Mohan buys a specific sofa lying ready in a shop and agrees to collect it and pay next week. That night the shop burns down without the seller's fault. The loss falls on:
options: The seller, since the sofa was still in his shop
Mohan, as ownership passed when the contract was made (Section 20) and risk goes with it
Both equally
The insurer only
mcq.explain: Under Section 20, in an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed. Section 26 makes risk follow property. So Mohan, already the owner, bears the loss and must pay the price.
mcq.topic: Passing of property in specific and ascertained goods (Sections 18 to 22)
mcq.fast: Specific + deliverable + unconditional = ownership at contract; delivery date is irrelevant.

mcq.q: A seller agrees to sell a specific heap of rice in deliverable state at ₹40 per kg; the heap has to be weighed to find the price. Ownership passes:
options: When the contract is made
When the heap is weighed and the buyer has notice of it — Section 22
When the price is paid
When the rice is delivered
mcq.explain: Section 22 says that where specific goods in a deliverable state must still be weighed, measured or tested by the seller to fix the price, property does not pass until that is done and the buyer has notice of it. Weighing is needed to fix the price here.
mcq.topic: Passing of property in specific and ascertained goods (Sections 18 to 22)
mcq.fast: Seller still must weigh/measure/test to fix price -> passes after that + notice.

mcq.q: Goods are sent to Leela "on approval" for 7 days. She neither approves nor rejects but keeps them for 15 days. Ownership:
options: Has not passed until she says "I approve"
Never passes in such cases
Has passed to her, because she kept them beyond the time fixed — Section 24
Passes only on payment
mcq.explain: Under Section 24, in a sale on approval or "sale or return", property passes when the buyer signifies approval, does an act adopting the transaction, or keeps the goods beyond the time fixed without giving notice of rejection (or beyond a reasonable time if none is fixed).
mcq.topic: Unascertained goods, approval and right of disposal (Sections 23 to 25)
mcq.fast: On approval: approve, adopt, or keep beyond the time = ownership passes.

mcq.q: A thief sells a stolen watch to Ritu, who buys it in good faith for value. The true owner finds it. The owner:
options: Cannot recover it, as Ritu bought in good faith
Can recover only if he pays Ritu her price
Can recover it, as a seller who is not the owner cannot pass a better title — Section 27
Can claim only damages from Ritu
mcq.explain: Section 27 lays down the rule "nemo dat quod non habet": where goods are sold by a person who is not their owner and has no authority, the buyer gets no better title than the seller had. A thief has no title at all, so Ritu gets none, even though she acted honestly. She may sue the thief.
mcq.topic: Transfer of title by non-owners (Sections 27 to 30)
mcq.fast: Thief has no title -> nobody after him gets title (nemo dat).

mcq.q: Raj obtains goods from Sohan by fraud, and before Sohan cancels the contract, Raj sells them to Vimal, who buys in good faith without notice. Vimal:
options: Gets no title, as Raj obtained the goods by fraud
Must return the goods to Sohan
Gets title only if he pays again
Gets a good title — Section 29
mcq.explain: A contract induced by fraud is voidable, not void, so Raj had a voidable title. Section 29 provides that a buyer who acquires goods from such a seller in good faith and without notice, before the contract has been rescinded, gets a good title. Sohan's remedy lies against Raj.
mcq.topic: Transfer of title by non-owners (Sections 27 to 30)
mcq.fast: Voidable title + resale BEFORE rescission + good-faith buyer = good title.

mcq.q: Kiran orders 100 bags of cement; the seller delivers 120 bags. Under Section 37, Kiran may:
options: Only reject all 120
Accept 100 and reject 20, reject all 120, or accept all 120 at the contract rate
Only accept 100
Accept 120 but pay for 100
mcq.explain: Section 37(2) gives the buyer three choices when a larger quantity is delivered: accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, reject the whole, or accept the whole and pay for it at the contract rate. He cannot keep the excess free of charge.
mcq.topic: Wrong quantity, instalments, carriers, examination (Sections 37 to 41)
mcq.fast: Excess delivery: three options — take the right qty, reject all, or take all at contract rate.

mcq.q: Unless otherwise agreed, the buyer of goods is NOT bound to accept delivery:
options: At the seller's place of business
By instalments — Section 38
During business hours
In a deliverable state
mcq.explain: Section 38 says a buyer need not take delivery in parts unless he agreed to it. The other choices describe normal rules of delivery under Sections 36 — goods are generally delivered where they are, at a reasonable hour, and in a deliverable state.
mcq.topic: Performance: duties and rules of delivery (Sections 31 to 36)

mcq.q: If the contract says nothing about the place of delivery, specific goods sold are to be delivered:
options: At the buyer's residence
At the nearest railway station
Wherever the goods lie when sold — Section 36
At the place chosen by the buyer
mcq.explain: Section 36(1): unless the contract says otherwise, goods already sold are handed over wherever they happen to be when sold; for goods merely agreed to be sold, the place is where they lie when the agreement is made, or where they are made if they did not then exist. The seller need not carry them to the buyer.
mcq.topic: Performance: duties and rules of delivery (Sections 31 to 36)
mcq.fast: No agreed place = where the goods are.

mcq.q: Under Section 42, a buyer is deemed to have accepted goods when he:
options: Opens the parcel to examine them
Asks for more time to examine them
Keeps them beyond a reasonable time without telling the seller he rejects them
Receives them at his warehouse for examination
mcq.explain: Section 42 treats the buyer as having accepted the goods when he tells the seller so, when he does an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership after delivery, or when he keeps them for more than a reasonable time without intimating rejection. Mere receipt or examination is not acceptance (Section 41 gives a right to examine).
mcq.fast: Acceptance = say so, act like owner, or keep too long silently.

mcq.q: A buyer rightfully refuses to accept goods delivered to him. He:
options: Must return them at his own cost
Must sell them and send the money
Need not return them; it is enough to tell the seller he refuses them — Section 43
Must keep them for one year
mcq.explain: Under Section 43, unless agreed otherwise, a buyer who rightly rejects delivered goods has no duty to send them back; telling the seller is enough, and it is then for the seller to arrange to take the goods back. Telling the seller clearly that he rejects them is enough.
mcq.fast: Rightful rejection: just inform — no duty to send back.
